Sample text:
---
# On Maps

A good map is a carefully chosen lie.

The London Underground map is the famous example. Harry Beck drew it in 1931 by ignoring geography almost entirely. The real tunnels wobble and sprawl, and stations that look neighbors on paper may be a mile apart on the surface. Beck straightened everything into lines at 45 and 90 degrees and spaced the stations evenly. Any surveyor would call it wrong, yet millions of people have used it to get where they were going. It works because it discards what a traveler doesn't need. Underground, you don't care about the curve of the street above you. You care about where to change trains.

This seems true of understanding in general. To know something is to have a good enough compression of it, one that throws away the right things. A map as detailed as the territory, as Borges joked, would be useless. It would need its own map.

What interests me is that every compression has an angle. A road map and a geological map of the same valley are both accurate, and they'd barely recognize each other. One says *here is how to pass through*. The other says *here is what it's made of, and how it got that way*. Neither is the valley. And the person who made each one was answering a question, even if they never wrote it down.

So when I feel suspicious of some confident summary, whether of a person, a historical era, or a scientific field, the useful question is rarely "is this true?" It's "what was this drawn to help someone do?" A personality type describes a person for the purpose of predicting them. A résumé describes a life for the purpose of hiring. A eulogy describes a life for the purpose of grief. All of them are accurate and all of them are lies of omission, and it would be a mistake to demand that any one of them be the whole thing.

There's a quieter consequence, which is that we live inside maps we forgot we drew. "Morning person." "Bad at math." "The kind of place this is." These began as useful sketches, and somewhere along the way they hardened into terrain. Much of growing up, or changing your mind, is noticing the edge of a map you'd mistaken for the world and stepping past it. Old cartographers wrote *here be dragons* at those edges, though I suspect the more honest ones simply left the space blank.

I like the blank space. It's the most truthful thing a map can offer: *nobody here has looked closely yet.* It's an invitation as much as a limit.

If I could ask one thing of every explanation I meet, it would be a small courtesy: mark your edges. Say what you left out and what you were for. A map that admits it's a map is one I can trust far more than one insisting it's the ground.

And then, having trusted it, I'd still like to go walk the valley myself.
---

## Sample kind
GENERIC_ESSAY — A polished, thesis-driven essay develops a clear argument through an extended map metaphor, with some stylistic color but little personal disclosure.

## Grounded reading
The voice is composed and inviting, turning a familiar transit map into a way to think about understanding, identity, and explanation. Its central pathos is gentle suspicion toward accounts that present themselves as complete: summaries can help us navigate, but they also leave things out and can harden into limits. The invitation is to notice those edges, ask what an explanation is for, and remain open to experience beyond it.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds maps as purposeful omissions, the angle built into every account, and labels that can be mistaken for reality. It gives special weight to blank space as both an honest admission of what is unknown and an invitation to look more closely, ending with the desire to walk the valley rather than rely on its representation.

## Evidence line
> A good map is a carefully chosen lie.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay is coherent and repeatedly returns to the same distinctive map-and-blank-space imagery, while its claims and polished explanatory style remain broadly familiar.
